practical.title: Personalized Greeting Program
objectives: Understand the fundamental structure of a basic C program.
Write, compile, and execute a "Hello, World!" program using a command-line compiler.
Explain the purpose of `#include <stdio.h>` and the `main` function.
Identify and correctly use the `printf` function for outputting text to the console.
Recognize common syntax errors in C and understand the compilation process.
learningObjectives: Understand the fundamental structure of a basic C program.
Write, compile, and execute a "Hello, World!" program using a command-line compiler.
Explain the purpose of `#include <stdio.h>` and the `main` function.
Identify and correctly use the `printf` function for outputting text to the console.
Recognize common syntax errors in C and understand the compilation process.

coachingPrompts: What do you predict will happen before you run it?
What evidence shows that your change worked?
Can you explain the result in your own words?

teachingPlaylist.title: Run the baseline program
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Before changing any code, compile and run the provided greeting.c to see the baseline output. This establishes a known-good starting point so you can observe the exact effect of your edits later. In the terminal, run: clang greeting.c -o greeting && ./greeting. Note the printed line and whether the cursor moves to a new line (because of the \n). Observing the baseline helps you reason about subsequent changes and builds confidence that your toolchain is working.

teachingPlaylist.title: Modify the printf to a personalized greeting
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Understand Modify the printf to a personalized greeting.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Edit the string inside printf to greet yourself or a friend. This is a safe, low-risk change that will immediately show up when you recompile. Think of the string literal as the program speaking; changing it is like giving the program a new line to say. Save your edit and re-run the compile-and-run commands. Observe that only the text changed — program structure and behavior remain identical. This step reinforces how small code edits translate into visible output changes.

teachingPlaylist.title: Experiment: remove the newline and restore it
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Understand Experiment: remove the newline and restore it.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Now deliberately remove the \n inside your printf and recompile. Observe what happens to subsequent terminal output — the cursor will remain on the same line after your greeting. This small change demonstrates how escape sequences control formatting. Restore the \n afterward. This is also an opportunity to practice the edit-compile-run loop and to learn to interpret output placement as a clue to string formatting.

teachingPlaylist.title: Optional: Remove a semicolon and observe the compiler error
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Understand Optional: Remove a semicolon and observe the compiler error.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Carefully remove the semicolon at the end of the printf line (or another statement) and attempt to compile. The compiler will produce an error that can be a bit cryptic at first; read it and identify the reported line number and message. This is intentional practice: compiler messages are diagnostic tools that guide you to the fix. After observing the error, restore the semicolon and compile successfully.

codeWalkthrough.speakerText: This directive includes the standard input/output header which declares printf and other I/O functions.
codeWalkthrough.explanation: Makes I/O functions available to the compiler.

codeWalkthrough.speakerText: This line declares the main function which is the entry point for every C program.
codeWalkthrough.explanation: Execution begins at main; int indicates it returns a status code.

codeWalkthrough.speakerText: Curly braces open the function body; everything inside runs when the program starts.
codeWalkthrough.explanation: Start of the main function's code block.

codeWalkthrough.speakerText: This printf call prints text to the console; the string is a literal and \n is the newline escape.
codeWalkthrough.explanation: Function call that produces visible output when program runs.

codeWalkthrough.speakerText: return 0 tells the operating system the program finished successfully.
codeWalkthrough.explanation: Standard convention to indicate success to the caller.

codeWalkthrough.speakerText: Closing brace ends the main function and the program; compilation will translate this into machine code.
codeWalkthrough.explanation: End of the function's code block.
